doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Rock and roll, Canada and country and western
summary: Jeannie turned professional in 1950; rock and roll hurt work so they played Toronto and Quebec, where they saw Dizzy, until country and western took over.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You guys started playing professionally about what time?
That’s standard hours, I know. More than that and we get overtime, right? I mean was it in the mid to late 50s that you started playing?
I think I can say that I was a professional in 1950. That is in jazz music and classical music.
I was just wondering if the rock & roll era, and the British invasion of rock & roll and Elvis and all of that, if it affected your employment. © Fillius Jazz Archive -30-

It did, it did. That’s why we were slick enough to go to Canada. Because Canada was twenty years behind the United States. Exactly twenty years. So when we went to Canada, we were like heroes and they really thought that we were the cat’s meow. And we could play Duke Ellington and we could play Count Basie, and could play, of course we did, we had to do “Blueberry Hill” — Fats Domino, they’d say in Quebec. But by the same time Louis Armstrong had a hit on “Blueberry Hill” also. And although we threw in some of those kind of songs, we’d always do jazz. We’d always do “Cherokee” like for the band tune, and take fours. And they’d all be amazed. In fact, that’s where I saw Dizzy, about the same thing, because his band was staying in the same hotel we were during that time when nobody could get arrested in the United States. You’d go to Toronto or go to Quebec City. That was like going to Europe. So we were smart enough to kind of move ourselves around. You only had to come out, like about every three or six months you had to come out for two weeks, or become a citizen or something like that. And that’s why a lot of times we’d come to Buffalo and hang out with the jam sessions and whatever.

Yeah, on Sunday. So that extended our time. Because everybody else was getting killed. We had one short period in, I’ll say about 1954, when we were in Canada and we almost got clobbered in Canada. The Queen came over and she had decided she loved country & western. And for a short time, that’s all there was in Toronto, and every joint but ours was country & western people, even though they were from New York. But the Canadians didn’t know that. You know these guys come in there from New York because if you’ve got a red guitar and sing “Red River Valley” you could get a gig in Toronto. And this is true — the whole country went country. It’s true. And we had to wait that out. Rock & roll in the United States and country & western, for a while there we didn’t work too good.
